name: Robot Lawn Mowers
hub_intro: Irish grass grows nine months a year and rains don't pause it — which makes the robot mower arguably more useful here than anywhere. The new wire-free generation (GPS/vision navigation) removed the old installation pain, and prices now start under €600. Constant micro-mowing also means clippings vanish as mulch and lawns visibly thicken. We compare wire and wire-free options for every garden size.
guide: Traditional robots need a perimeter wire buried around the lawn — €100–300 of installation or a weekend of your knees. New RTK-GPS and vision models map boundaries from an app walk-around. If your budget allows, go wire-free: relocation, repairs and layout changes become trivial.

Quoted capacity assumes ideal flat lawns and daily runs. Slopes, narrow passages, trees and complex shapes eat capacity. Measure your actual grass area (apps or Google Maps work) and buy the next size up — an under-specced robot leaves mohawks.
Mulching is the secret lawn upgrade

Robots cut a few millimetres daily and drop the dust-sized clippings as mulch — feeding the lawn continuously. Owners consistently report thicker, greener grass within a season, with no clippings to collect, bag or dump. It's lawn care that compounds.

All serious robots mow happily in Irish drizzle (most park themselves in heavy rain). Check slope ratings against your garden: 25–35% covers typical suburban gradients; banks and ditches need specialist models. Wet long grass in spring growth spurts may need a catch-up manual cut.

faqs.q: Do robot lawn mowers work in Irish rain?
faqs.a: Yes — they're built for Northern European weather and mow fine in drizzle and light rain. Most have rain sensors that pause heavy-rain sessions (cutting wet grass clumps), then resume. Daily mowing schedules mean a paused day never matters.

faqs.q: Do I need to bury a perimeter wire?
faqs.a: Only on traditional models. The current wire-free generation (Segway Navimow, Husqvarna EPOS, Worx Vision) maps your lawn via satellite positioning or cameras from a simple app walk-around. Wire models remain cheaper for simple lawns; wire-free wins for everything else.

faqs.q: How much lawn can a robot mower handle?
faqs.a: Models are rated 400 m² to 5,000 m²+. A typical Irish suburban back garden (100–300 m²) is easy territory; rated capacity matters more for rural homes and corner sites. Complex shapes and slopes effectively shrink rated capacity ~20%.

faqs.q: What about clippings — do I need to collect them?
faqs.a: No — robots mulch. Cutting daily means clippings are millimetre dust that drops into the sward, feeding it. No collection, no brown bin runs, and a measurably thicker lawn within a season. Spring growth spurts may briefly outpace mulching.

faqs.q: Are robot mowers safe with children and pets?
faqs.a: Modern units stop blades instantly on lift or tilt, have collision sensors, and the premium tier adds camera object detection. Blades are small pivoting razors, not mower blades. Standard sense applies: schedule around toddler garden hours; hedgehog-friendly night-off settings are recommended.

Rarely — they're poor theft targets: PIN-locked, GPS-tracked, geofenced (alarm + useless off their home base) and brand-flagged. Most insurers treat them as garden contents; registration and a gate latch do the rest.

faqs.q: How much maintenance do they need?
faqs.a: Minutes per month: flip and rinse the deck occasionally, swap the €10–15 blade set every 1–3 months, winter-store the base station if hard frosts threaten. Compare with petrol servicing, fuel runs and an hour of your weekend, weekly.

faqs.q: Robot mower vs paying someone to cut grass?
faqs.a: A €25/cut service fortnightly across an Irish March–October season runs €350–450/year, every year. A €700 robot plus ~€40/year consumables overtakes it inside two seasons — and mows daily instead of fortnightly. The maths rarely favours the van.

pages.intro: Nine months of growing season makes Ireland robot-mower heaven, and the technology finally matches the need: wire-free navigation, app boundaries, rain intelligence. products.name: Segway Navimow i105E
pros: No-wire setup in under an hour
Neat parallel lines, not random wandering
cons: Needs decent sky view for GPS
500 m² cap — bigger gardens pay more
products.verdict: The robot mower for normal humans: unbox, walk the boundary with your phone, done. For typical Irish suburban gardens it's the new default answer.

products.name: Husqvarna Automower 305
pros: Two decades of robotic mowing pedigree
products.verdict: The Toyota Hilux of robot mowers: wire setup is the toll, then a decade of dependable daily cutting. Sloped or awkward gardens especially benefit.

products.name: Worx Landroid Vision M600
pros: Works under heavy tree cover (no GPS needed)
products.verdict: The answer for gardens GPS can't see: dense trees, high walls, narrow side passages. Camera navigation plus hedgehog-grade detection is a genuinely Irish-garden-friendly combination.

products.name: Gardena Sileno City 250
products.verdict: City gardens under 250 m² need nothing more: near-silent, compact, reliable, €599. The wire install in a small garden is one podcast long.

products.name: Segway Navimow i110E
pros: Same friendly setup as the i105
products.verdict: The large-garden sweet spot: country-home lawn coverage without a contractor visit or a spool of wire. Two lawns, one robot, one app.

The small-garden class costs €500–800, runs quiet enough for evening cuts, and squeezes through gaps big robots refuse. Five compact options, including wire-free picks, ranked on small-space intelligence.

products.name: Gardena Sileno City 250 (Small)
products.verdict: Purpose-built for exactly the Irish estate garden: narrow side strips, modest lawns, close neighbours. It just quietly works, year after year.

products.name: Segway Navimow i105E (Small)
pros: Zero installation — renters can even take it along
products.verdict: Pay the €200 wire-free premium and boundary changes, new flowerbeds or moving house become app edits. The flexible small-garden choice.

products.name: Worx Landroid S300
pros: Offset blade cuts closer to edges than anyone
products.verdict: The tinkerer's small robot: edge-hugging cuts reduce strimming, the app is full-featured, and upgrade modules grow with your needs.

products.name: Flymo EasiLife GO 250
products.verdict: The recognisable-brand budget route: underneath the orange plastic is Husqvarna group tech. Flat small lawns get reliable robot mowing at the category's floor price.

products.name: Bosch Indego S+ 350
pros: Maps and mows in efficient lanes, not random
products.verdict: The efficiency pick: systematic lanes finish the lawn in half the time of random-pattern rivals, meaning more quiet hours and less battery wear.

Setup measured in minutes per zone

pages.intro: The perimeter wire was robot mowing's original sin: a buried installation that punished every garden change and snapped at the worst moments. This page compares pure wire-free options across budgets, including which navigation tech suits which Irish garden.

products.name: Segway Navimow i105E (Wire-Free)
pros: The wire-free experience perfected at volume price
Vision fills GPS shadows near walls
cons: Heavy tree canopy still challenges it

Fastest setup in the entire category

products.verdict: For the gardens other robots refuse: steep banks, rough ground, split lawns across gravel. The AWD specialist that treats Irish rural terrain as intended use.
